title: Post-Transcriptional Regulation of Regenerative, Low-Scar, and Fibrotic Wound Repair
content: Some developmental and tissue-specific wounds heal with minimal fibrosis and substantial restoration of tissue structure. In this review, we examine RNA-level regulation of scarless, low-scar, and regenerative healing in fetal skin, oral mucosa, cornea, zebrafish heart, and other mammalian and fibrotic comparators. We prioritize mechanisms tested causally in vivo and distinguish these findings from associative profiling and extrapolations from normally scar-forming wounds. We focus on microRNA (miRNA) circuits that regulate inflammatory resolution, epithelial migration, fibroblast activation and persistence/exit, extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition and remodeling, and regenerative proliferation. We also assess alternative RNA processing, lncRNAs/circRNAs, RNA-binding proteins, translational control, m6A regulation, and extracellular-vesicle-mediated RNA transfer. We distinguish endogenous post-transcriptional effects from transcriptionally initiated isoform expression and exogenous RNA therapies, and identify TGF-β/SMAD signaling and collagen organization as key downstream convergence points. Across studies, extensive evidence shows that post-transcriptional regulation shapes repair processes, while substantial experimental evidence demonstrates that RNA-level interventions alter fibrosis, scarring, or regenerative responses. However, direct evidence that endogenous post-transcriptional mechanisms determine regenerative versus fibrotic outcomes remains limited. Regenerative cardiac studies implicate specific RNA-associated regulators in injury-induced proliferation and regeneration, but their mechanisms sometimes involve transcriptionally initiated isoform expression, and their effects do not necessarily determine overall repair fate. We therefore propose a phase-resolved framework linking RNA regulators to defined repair processes, tissue-level outcomes, and the strength of causal evidence for regenerative versus fibrotic trajectories.
